learn: Everything around us is made of materials, like wood, metal, plastic, glass, paper and cloth.
A chair might be made of wood. A spoon might be made of metal.
One object can be made of more than one material: a pencil has wood, graphite, metal and rubber.
check: A spoon is often made of...
Can one object be made of more than one material?
lessons.try: Pick three objects and list the materials in each.

learn: Properties describe what a material is like.
Colour, texture, hardness, flexibility and whether it floats or sinks are properties.
Metal is hard and strong. Rubber is flexible and bouncy.
lessons.try: Test five objects to see which float and which sink in a bowl of water.

learn: Engineers choose materials whose properties fit the job.
A raincoat needs a waterproof material, like plastic. A window needs a transparent one, like glass.
Using the wrong material can make an object fail: a paper umbrella would get soggy.
check: A raincoat needs a material that is...
Why wouldn't a paper umbrella work?
A window needs a material that is...
lessons.try: Design a cup for hot cocoa. Which material would you choose and why?

learn: Matter is anything that takes up space and has mass.
A solid keeps its own shape. A block, a rock and an ice cube are solids.
A solid stays the same shape even if you put it in a different container.
check: Anything that takes up space and has mass
Takes the shape of its container
lessons.try: Put a block in a cup, then in a bowl. Did its shape change?

learn: A liquid flows and takes the shape of its container.
Water, milk and juice are liquids.
A liquid keeps the same amount even when poured into a different shape of container.
check: A liquid takes the shape of its...
When poured, the amount of liquid...
lessons.try: Pour one cup of water into a tall glass and then a wide bowl. Is it still one cup?

learn: A gas spreads out to fill whatever space it is in.
Air is a mix of gases. You can't see it, but you can feel it as wind.
Blowing up a balloon fills it with gas.
check: Spreads out to fill its space
What fills a balloon when you blow it up?
lessons.try: Blow up a balloon. What is inside it?

learn: Heating a solid can make it melt into a liquid. Ice melts into water.
Cooling a liquid can make it freeze into a solid. Water freezes into ice.
Butter and chocolate melt when warm, too.
lessons.try: Put an ice cube on a plate in the sun and one in the shade. Which melts first?

learn: Some changes can be reversed. Melted ice can be frozen again.
Melted chocolate can harden again when it cools.
These are called reversible changes.
check: Can melted ice be frozen again?
A change that can be undone is...
Melted chocolate cooling and hardening is...
lessons.try: Freeze water in a tray, let it melt, then freeze it again.

learn: Some changes can't be reversed. You can't un-bake a cake or un-cook an egg.
Burning paper turns it into ash and smoke for good.
These are called irreversible changes. Cooking should always be done with a grown-up.
check: Who should be with you when cooking?
lessons.try: With a grown-up, cook an egg. Can it go back to raw?

learn: Large objects can be built from many small pieces.
A wall is made of many bricks. A house can be built from logs or blocks.
Toy blocks can be built into a tower, then taken apart and built into a bridge.
check: What is a wall made of?
Can the same pieces build different things?
A tower of blocks can become a...
lessons.try: Build something with blocks, then take it apart and build something new.

learn: When you take an object apart, you can see its pieces.
A puzzle is many pieces that fit together.
Scientists take things apart to learn how they work.
check: Why do scientists take things apart?
When you take an object apart, you see its...
lessons.try: With a grown-up, look at the parts of an old pen or a toy.

learn: A structure is something built to hold weight or stand up.
Wide bases make towers more stable. Triangles make structures strong.
Engineers test their structures and improve them.
check: What makes a tower more stable?
lessons.try: Build a paper tower that can hold a book. Test and improve it.

learn: Plants need sunlight to make their food.
A plant in a dark closet will turn yellow and weak.
Plants often bend toward light.
check: What do plants need sunlight for?
A plant in the dark turns...
lessons.try: Put a plant near a window and watch it lean toward the light over a week.

learn: Plants need water. Roots take water from the soil.
Too little water makes plants wilt. Too much can rot roots.
Soil gives plants nutrients and holds them steady.
check: What do roots take from the soil?
What happens with too little water?
lessons.try: Grow two bean seeds: water one, don't water the other. Compare.

learn: Plants need air and room to grow.
Leaves take in a gas from the air called carbon dioxide.
Crowded plants compete for light, water and space.
check: What gas do leaves take from the air?
Do plants need room to grow?
lessons.try: Plant seeds close together and far apart. Which grow better?

learn: Flowers make pollen, a yellow powder.
Bees, butterflies, hummingbirds and bats carry pollen from flower to flower.
Moving pollen helps flowers make seeds. This is pollination.
lessons.try: Watch a flowering plant for five minutes. What visitors come?

learn: Seeds travel to new places to grow.
Dandelion seeds float on the wind. Burrs stick to animal fur. Coconuts float on water.
Animals eat fruits and drop the seeds far away.
lessons.try: Blow on a dandelion and watch the seeds travel.

learn: Scientists build models to understand how things work.
You can model a bee with a pipe cleaner: dip it in one flower's powder and touch another flower.
The model shows how pollen moves.
check: In the model, the cotton swab is like a...
lessons.try: Use a cotton swab and cocoa powder to model pollination between two paper flowers.

learn: A habitat is the place where a plant or animal lives.
It gives the living thing food, water and shelter.
Different living things need different habitats.
check: A habitat gives food, water and...
Do all living things need the same habitat?
lessons.try: Choose an animal and draw its habitat.

learn: Deserts are dry. Camels and cactuses live there.
Rainforests are wet and warm with many kinds of life, like monkeys and frogs.
Oceans are salty water homes for whales, fish and coral. Polar areas are icy, home to polar bears and penguins.
check: Which habitat is wet and warm with many kinds of life?
lessons.try: Sort animal pictures into desert, rainforest, ocean and polar.

learn: Biodiversity means the variety of living things in a place.
Some habitats, like rainforests, have huge biodiversity.
Scientists count and compare the living things in different places.
lessons.try: Count the different kinds of plants and bugs in a small patch of yard.

learn: Earth has many landforms: mountains, hills, valleys, plains, canyons and islands.
A canyon is a deep valley with steep sides, often cut by a river.
Maps can show where landforms are.
check: A deep valley with steep sides is a...
What can show where landforms are?
lessons.try: Model a mountain and a valley with sand or clay.

learn: Oceans are salt water. Most lakes and rivers are fresh water.
Water on Earth can be liquid or solid, like glaciers and ice caps.
Most of Earth's water is salty ocean water.
check: A glacier is water as a...
Where is most of Earth's water?
lessons.try: Taste a drop of salt water and a drop of fresh water (with a grown-up).

lessons.t: Making Maps of Land and Water
learn: Maps use colours and symbols: blue for water, green for low land, brown for mountains.
A map key explains the colours.
You can model a place and then draw its map from above.
check: What colour often shows water on a map?
What explains the colours on a map?
A map shows a place from...
lessons.try: Draw a map of a pretend island with a mountain, a lake and a river.

learn: Some changes to Earth take a very long time.
Wind and water slowly wear rock away. This is weathering and erosion.
The Grand Canyon was carved by a river over millions of years.
check: Wearing rock away by wind and water is...
Do these changes take a long time?
lessons.try: Rub two rocks together. Look at the dust: that's what weathering makes.

learn: Some changes happen quickly.
Earthquakes shake the ground. Volcanoes erupt with lava. Floods and landslides move land fast.
These events can change land in minutes or hours.
check: What comes out of an erupting volcano?
lessons.try: Make a model landslide by tilting a tray of wet sand.

learn: People design ways to slow down erosion.
Planting grass and trees holds soil in place with their roots.
Walls and fences can block wind and water.
check: What can block wind and water?
lessons.try: Test: pour water on bare soil and on soil with grass. Which washes away more?

learn: Engineers start by asking: what is the problem? Who has it?
They list what the solution must do.
For example: "The plant tips over. We need a pot that stays up."
check: Engineers list what the solution must...
Who has the problem is part of...
lessons.try: Find a small problem at home and describe it clearly.

learn: Engineers sketch many ideas before they build.
Labels show the parts and materials.
Sharing sketches with others brings more ideas.
lessons.try: Sketch two ideas for solving your problem. Label them.

learn: Build your best idea and test it.
Compare two designs fairly: test them the same way.
Use what you learn to improve your design.
check: How should you compare two designs?
What do you do after testing?
lessons.try: Build two paper boats and test which holds more pennies.
